investigate:theory.summary:
Theory lens on moving the array. Scripts and results are in the scratch folder (files below); no repository file was changed. The three parallel studies (array3d, band_plan, topology .md) did not exist yet when I looked, so I only checked topology_study.py to avoid repeating its u-v rotation-synthesis demo.

**Model.** An orientation is a rotation matrix R(t) in SO(3) (store it as a unit quaternion). Element n sits at R(t)p_n, so its phase for a source in unit direction u is k·u·R(t)p_n. Rotating the array is the same as rotating the source the other way in the array frame, and each element traces a curve on a sphere of radius |p_n|. Motion never makes the aperture larger than the array's own radius; it fills it, and changes which directions the aperture is projected onto.

**Two ways to combine K orientations.**
- **Non-coherent** (add per-orientation spectra or Fisher matrices): needs only a source that stays put. Information adds, and sidelobes average but do not cancel.
- **Coherent** (a true synthetic aperture): needs a phase reference that does not move, such as an element on the rotation axis or a fixed antenna on one of the four channels.

**Main results.**
- **Turntable under the single 225 mm ring of 8** (sources 20-30° up, azimuth-only estimator, 64 snapshots in total): gross errors fall from 17 / 66 / 76 % at 1.6 / 2.0 / 2.3 GHz with no rotation to 0 / 0 / 1.7 % with 8 orientations. A static elevation-aware (2-D) estimator gives 0 % at all three, so software fixes this failure better than a motor.
- **Calibration residuals average out.** They are fixed in the array frame, so a full turn cut the 95th-percentile error from 1.20° to 0.49° (1 GHz, 5° residual, 8 orientations).
- **Elevation near the horizon.** For a planar array the Fisher information splits into a part across the normal (full) and a part towards it, which scales as cos²γ (γ = angle from the normal). A horizontal plate therefore has zero elevation information at the horizon, and spinning it about the vertical adds none. Elevation CRLB for the 16-whip plate at 1 GHz (20 dB, 64 snapshots, noise only): 0.55° at 5° elevation and unbounded at 0° when flat; 0.095° with the plate tilted 30° and spun.
- **Tilt 54.7° and spin equals a full tumble.** For isotropic elements, a fixed tilt of arccos(1/√3) spun about the vertical gives exactly isotropic information, 2/3 of broadside in every direction. A uniform tumble over SO(3) gives the same (0.65-0.67 numerically). One motor and a wedge match the "gyroscopic" tumble for direction finding.
- **What the third axis adds.** Roll about boresight gives polarisation diversity and removes the zenith keyhole. The panel is linearly polarised, so power against roll angle ψ is ½(I + Q cos2ψ + U sin2ψ): three roll angles give I, Q and U. V needs a phase reference or a circular feed. The third axis adds no aperture, no SNR and no instantaneous coverage: under a uniform tumble the panel's ±60° cone sees any given direction 25 % of the time.
- **Path design for the panel** (upper hemisphere, worst-direction information in broadside looks): 12 poses coned at 30° tilt score 1.74; 12 Fibonacci az-el pointings score 1.05. With 24 poses, adding 0/60/120° roll lifts the worst-case polarisation metric from 0.03 to 2.15. The repo's `evolve` found nothing better than coning plus roll in 4,832 evaluations.
- **Continuous motion.** Doppler is ωr/λ: 1.9 Hz at 0.4 GHz and 10.8 Hz at 2.3 GHz for a whip at 225 mm and 60 rpm; 6.4 Hz at 5.8 GHz for the panel corner. That is useless as a Doppler direction finder (500 Hz deviation at 0.4 GHz would need about 16,000 rpm), which is why pseudo-Doppler switches electronically. What matters is phase slew: 3.9°/ms at 2.3 GHz and 60 rpm, so coherent blocks must stay under about 1.5 ms or be de-rotated with the known R(t). At 1 rpm the limit is 88 ms. Step-and-stare or 10 rpm or slower is the sensible regime.
- **Gyroscopic torque** is small: 0.15 N·m for a 1.5 kg, 500 mm plate (estimate) spun at 60 rpm and tilted at 30°/s; 1.5 N·m at 600 rpm. A 5 cm centre-of-gravity offset already costs 0.74 N·m.
- **Error budget.** Heading error maps one-to-one into azimuth bias. Position error costs 0.48 / 2.9 / 7.0° of phase per mm at 0.4 / 2.4 / 5.8 GHz. A 0.2° axis wobble is 0.4 / 2.3 / 5.5° at 225 mm radius (0.5° and 1.3° at the panel corner at 2.4 and 5.8 GHz). Hobby IMU heading (about 2° static, 3.5° dynamic) is worse than the 0.5° manifold target, so use shaft encoders. Flexed coax costs about ±2° up to 4 GHz and ±4° at 4-8 GHz, so the radios and core board should ride on the rotor.

findings.claim: Orientation is R(t) in SO(3), stored as a unit quaternion. Element n is at R(t)p_n and its phase is k u·R(t)p_n = k (R^T u)·p_n, so rotating the array equals counter-rotating the source in the array frame. Each element moves on a sphere of radius |p_n|, so the synthesised aperture is bounded by the array radius: 225 mm for the whips, 53 mm for the panel's 4x4 corner. Motion fills or re-projects the aperture; it does not enlarge it.

Non-coherent combining over K orientations (sum of a_k^H R_k a_k, or summed Fisher matrices) needs only a stationary source. Coherent synthesis of a K·N-element virtual array needs a phase reference that does not move with the elements: an element on the rotation axis, or a fixed antenna on one of the four channels, leaving three moving. Without it the source's own modulation and the LO phase between dwells destroy coherence.
findings.source: derivation; rotating arrays degrade superresolution unless motion-compensated: Zatman, Asilomar 2000, https://search.isc.ac/inventory/49/1743166.htm ; two-element rotating-baseline virtual circular array (R-MUSIC): https://doi.org/10.3390/fi6010155

findings.topic: Turntable under the single 225 mm ring of 8
findings.claim: Sources 20-30 deg up, azimuth-only Bartlett, 3 deg cal residual, 20 dB, 64 snapshots in total split over K orientations spread across 45 deg. Gross-error rate: 1.6 GHz 17.3 % (K=1) to 0 % (K>=2); 2.0 GHz 65.8 / 6.5 / 0.2 / 0 % for K=1/2/4/8; 2.3 GHz 75.5 / 26.3 / 14.2 / 1.7 / 2.3 % for K=1/2/4/8/16. A static 2-D (azimuth and elevation) estimator gives 0 % at all three frequencies with 95th percentile 0.60-0.70 deg. A 0.5 deg orientation error changes nothing material (95th percentile 0.77 deg at 2.3 GHz).

2.3 GHz, source 30 deg up, azimuth-only steering, ring of 8 at 225 mm. Highest sidelobe over mainlobe: 2.98 static (the wrong peak wins); non-coherent sum 1.60 / 1.22 / 0.91 for K=2/4/8, with no further gain beyond 8; coherent sum 0.56 for K>=4, equal to the filled-ring limit J0^2 (main 0.289, largest elsewhere 0.162). Rotation about the normal turns the 8-point ring into a continuous ring; it cannot beat the J0 pattern or repair the elevation mismatch itself.

Per-whip calibration errors are fixed in the array frame, so the DF bias they cause rotates with the array and averages down over a turn. At 1 GHz with a 5 deg residual, 30 dB and sources 0-15 deg up, the median / 95th percentile go from 0.41 / 1.20 deg static to 0.25 / 0.49 deg with 8 orientations over a full turn. Orientation-dependent multipath from the mount and ground should average the same way, but that was not simulated.

findings.topic: Fisher information of a moving planar array
findings.claim: For direction u with tangent basis T, J = 2·SNR·L·k^2 · sum over poses of T^T R S R^T T, where S = sum p p^T. For a rotationally symmetric planar array S = s(I - n n^T), giving eigenvalues s (across the normal) and s·cos^2(gamma) (towards the normal), gamma being the angle between u and the normal n. A horizontal plate has elevation information proportional to sin^2(el): zero at the horizon, plus an up/down mirror ambiguity. Spinning about the vertical leaves n unchanged and adds no elevation information.
findings.source: derivation; checked numerically in rot_theory.py (static and turntable both give worst-direction information 0.0 and elevation information 0.25 at 30 deg)

findings.topic: Elevation CRLB with tilt (two rings of 8, 225/112 mm)
findings.claim: 20 dB, 64 snapshots, noise only, averaged over a spin. At 1 GHz: flat plate, unbounded at el 0, 1.38 deg at 2 deg, 0.55 deg at 5 deg, 0.28 deg at 10 deg, 0.096 deg at 30 deg; tilted 15 deg, 0.19 deg at el 0; tilted 30 deg, 0.096 deg at el 0. At 0.4 GHz and el 5 deg: 1.38 deg flat, 0.24 deg at 30 deg tilt. At 2.3 GHz and el 5 deg: 0.24 deg flat, 0.041 deg at 30 deg tilt. Calibration residuals will dominate these noise-only figures in practice.

findings.topic: Magic-angle coning equals a full tumble
findings.claim: The average of (I - n n^T) over a uniform tumble on SO(3) is (2/3)I, so DF information is isotropic at 2/3 of broadside in every direction (numerical 0.65-0.67 with 2000 random poses). A fixed tilt of arccos(1/sqrt 3) = 54.7 deg spun about the vertical gives exactly the same (0.667 everywhere), because the cone average of n n^T is I/3. A 30 deg cone gives worst-direction 0.25 and mean 0.46. For isotropic elements, the full tumble adds nothing for DF over one motor and a fixed wedge.

Tumbling the 16-whip plate coherently (200 poses, 1 GHz) fills a ball of radius 225 mm. For a source in the plate's plane, the elevation half-power half-width drops from 46 deg (static, edge-on) to 23 deg, peak sidelobe -17.3 dB, the same in every direction and with no mirror ambiguity. A thin shell has point-spread sinc(2kr sin(delta/2)), first null near lambda/(2r). This needs the fixed phase reference; non-coherently only the Fisher result applies.

findings.topic: What the third axis adds and does not
findings.claim: SO(3) has three degrees of freedom: boresight direction (two) and roll about boresight (one). An az-el mount fixes roll as a function of pointing and has a keyhole at zenith, where the azimuth rate needed grows as 1/cos(el). Roll adds polarisation diversity for a linear panel, baseline rotation at fixed pointing, and keyhole-free tracking. It adds no aperture, no SNR and no instantaneous field of view: under a uniform tumble the +/-60 deg cone sees a given direction (1 - cos 60)/2 = 25 % of the time (numerical 0.250).
findings.source: derivation; keyhole: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyhole_problem ; tumble duty in rot_theory_results.json

findings.claim: For a linearly polarised panel rolled by psi, P(psi) = 1/2 (I + Q cos 2psi + U sin 2psi). Mismatch loss to a linear wave is cos^2(psi - psi0) (3 dB at 45 deg, a null at 90 deg); to a circular wave it is a constant 3 dB. Three roll angles (0/60/120 or 0/45/90) give I, Q, U; with K evenly spaced angles var(Q) = var(U) = 8 sigma^2/K and var(I) = 4 sigma^2/K. V (handedness) cannot be had from power through a linear element alone; it needs a phase reference between rolls or a circular or dual-polarised feed. Spinning vertical whips about the vertical gives no polarisation information; tilting them does mix polarisations.

findings.topic: Path design as optimisation (panel, upper hemisphere)
findings.claim: Metric: worst-direction DF information in units of one broadside look; +/-60 deg field of view with cos-gamma power gain. 12 poses: azimuth spin with boresight horizontal 0.0 (13.5 % of the hemisphere never seen); coning with boresight 30 deg up 1.74; Fibonacci az-el pointings 1.05. The repo's `evolve` reached 1.67 from the Fibonacci seed and did not improve on the coning seed in 4,832 evaluations. With 24 poses, coning gives 3.88; adding 0/60/120 deg roll leaves DF unchanged and lifts the worst-case Stokes design-matrix eigenvalue from 0.03 to 2.15 (Fibonacci plus roll: 0.51).

A three-ring gimbal loses a degree of freedom when two axes become parallel (middle ring at +/-90 deg); nearby, the rates needed scale as 1/cos(theta). Remedies: keep orientation as quaternions or matrices in software; limit the middle axis mechanically (Apollo warned at 70 deg and froze the platform at 85 deg); add a redundant fourth gimbal; or choose the axis order so the singular direction is one you do not need. For this project a tilt-then-spin mount with the tilt limited to about 60 deg never approaches lock.

Continuous rotation needs slip rings or RF rotary joints for 4-5 RF lines plus USB 3, unless everything rides on the rotor. Rotations in 3-D have a topological loophole: the anti-twister mechanism (Adams, US 3,586,413) passes a flexible cable to a continuously spinning platform with no slip ring by carrying the cable loop at half the platform speed. The simplest option is a limited-angle wrap (+/-180 or 360 deg, step-and-stare) or a battery, radios and small computer on the rotor.

v = omega x r and peak shift is omega·r/lambda. Whip at 225 mm: 1 rpm gives 0.03 Hz (0.4 GHz) and 0.18 Hz (2.3 GHz); 60 rpm gives 1.41 m/s, 1.9 and 10.8 Hz; 600 rpm gives 19 and 108 Hz. Panel corner at 53 mm: 60 rpm gives 2.7 Hz (2.4 GHz) and 6.4 Hz (5.8 GHz). Mechanical Doppler DF with 500 Hz deviation at 0.4 GHz and r = 225 mm would need about 1,670 rad/s, roughly 16,000 rpm; pseudo-Doppler gets the same effect by switching around a ring. With coherent channels the array measures phase directly and needs neither.

findings.topic: Coherent integration and snapshot switching under motion
findings.claim: Worst-case phase slew is k·r·omega. At 60 rpm: 3.9 deg/ms at 2.3 GHz (whip), 2.3 deg/ms at 5.8 GHz (panel corner), 0.68 deg/ms at 0.4 GHz. Blocks that stay under 0.1 rad of smear must be shorter than 1.5 ms, 2.5 ms and 8.4 ms respectively; at 10 rpm 8.8 ms (2.3 GHz) and at 1 rpm 88 ms. Longer integration, and the four slots of a 16-element snapshot cycle, must use a(theta, t) with the encoder-known R(t), which is exact for one source. Slot times of 15 us to 1 ms are harmless at 10 rpm or less. Step-and-stare avoids the issue.

findings.claim: Torque = I·omega_spin·Omega_tilt. For a 1.5 kg, 500 mm disc (mass and shape are estimates) I = 0.047 kg·m^2: spinning at 60 rpm and tilting at 30 deg/s gives 0.15 N·m (0.46 N·m at 90 deg/s); at 600 rpm, 1.5 N·m at 30 deg/s. Rim acceleration is about 1 g at 60 rpm and 100 g at 600 rpm. A 5 cm centre-of-gravity offset gives a static gravity torque of 0.74 N·m, larger than the gyroscopic term at any sensible rate. Balance the payload and stay at or below about 60 rpm.
findings.source: estimate: thin-disc inertia with assumed 1.5 kg mass; /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ascalva--claude-spares-spare-iFcbz1/8b6bf486-3081-448c-8f46-b00ba3ebceb0/scratchpad/rotation/rot_theory_results.json (torque)

findings.claim: An error delta about the vertical axis is an azimuth bias of exactly delta. A tilt error delta of the normal gives an elevation bias up to delta and an azimuth bias up to delta·tan(el). The AS5600 magnetic encoder resolves 360/4096 = 0.088 deg; a search result quotes a system INL of about +/-1 deg before linearisation, which I did not confirm against the datasheet table, so calibrate it against the turntable. BNO08x fused heading is listed at 2.0 deg static, 3.5 deg dynamic, and 0.5 deg/min drift in gaming mode. That is worse than the 0.5 deg manifold target, so shaft encoders should carry the budget, with an IMU only for tilt sanity checks.
findings.source: derivation; AS5600: https://www.infineon.com/assets/row/public/documents/24/49/infineon-as5600-datasheet-en.pdf ; BNO086 figures as listed at https://www.sparkfun.com/products/22857

findings.topic: Wobble, vibration and position error into phase
findings.claim: Phase error is 360·delta_r/lambda: 0.48 / 2.88 / 6.96 deg per mm at 0.4 / 2.4 / 5.8 GHz, so a 3 deg budget is 6.3 / 1.0 / 0.43 mm. Axis wobble of 0.2 deg at 225 mm radius (0.79 mm) is 0.38 / 2.3 / 5.5 deg; at the panel corner (53 mm) it is 0.09 / 0.53 / 1.3 deg. Sinusoidal vibration of 0.1 mm amplitude gives a phase-modulation index of 2·pi·a/lambda = 0.0008 / 0.005 / 0.012 rad, sidebands at -68 / -52 / -44 dBc. Rigid common-mode translation is a common phase and drops out for simultaneous channels, but appears as slot-to-slot phase under snapshot switching.

One flexible-assembly specification allows a phase change with flexure of +/-2 deg up to 4 GHz, +/-4 deg at 4-8 GHz and +/-6 deg at 8-18 GHz; ordinary cable is quoted at 5-20 deg per flexure at 10 GHz. Any RF cable that flexes outside the calibration loop adds an orientation-dependent error of that order. In rev B the tile-to-core jumpers are inside the PN calibration loop (recalibrate at each pose, 5-20 ms), but whip cables are outside it. Mount the plate, core and radios on the rotor so only USB and power cross the joint.

The turntable manifold is a(R^T u) only in free space. With a mast, mount and ground the true response is a(u, R): scattering changes with orientation. REDESIGN.md's own figure is that a -10 dB bounce moves phases by +/-18 deg, and tilting changes the ground-bounce geometry and the whips' ground-plane image. Either measure the manifold with the mount attached, per tilt, or rely on averaging over orientations. All K-orientation combining assumes the emitter is on and stationary for K·(move + settle + dwell); bursty emitters give one orientation per burst and can only be combined non-coherently.

open_questions: Is a non-rotating phase reference acceptable (an on-axis receive element, or one of the four channels on a fixed antenna)? Without it only non-coherent combining is available and the 3-D shell aperture result does not apply.

Real whips tilted 30-55 deg over a finite plate have pattern nulls, polarisation mixing and a changed ground image; the Fisher results assume isotropic elements and need a pattern-aware re-run (NEC or openEMS).

The panel coning tilt (30 deg) was a hand choice and was not swept; the path optimisation used 12-24 discrete poses and a hard +/-60 deg field of view, not a continuous trajectory with slew-rate and cable-wrap limits or an information-per-second objective.
The 1.7-2.3 % residual gross errors at 2.3 GHz with 8-16 non-coherent orientations come from the azimuth-only estimator's elevation mismatch; a 2-D estimator combined with rotation was not simulated.
Averaging of orientation-dependent multipath (mast, ground) under rotation is argued but not simulated; it needs a scatterer model or a measurement.

Cable strategy is undecided: everything on the rotor with battery and wireless or USB wrap, a limited-angle wrap, slip ring, or anti-twister loop. The 320 MB/s four-radio USB 3 stream across a moving joint is the hard part.
The AS5600 INL figure (about +/-1 deg) came from a garbled search snippet and was not confirmed against the datasheet table; stepper and gear backlash figures were not sourced.

The parallel studies (array3d_study.md, band_plan_study.md, topology_study.md) were not yet written when this ran, so overlap with their rotator and rotation-synthesis sections has not been reconciled.

investigate:simulate.summary:
Simulation lens complete. The script /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/rotation_study.py (a draft already existed from an interrupted earlier pass; I reviewed it, added a hemisphere-prior case and ran it in full: 1178 s, OMP_NUM_THREADS=3) writes tables.md, results.json and two plots into /Users/ascalva/Documents/code/sdr_array/array16/experiments/rotation/. No existing repo file was modified. No external facts are used; everything is Monte Carlo output or derivation, with model assumptions marked as estimates.

Cross-check: the K=1 azimuth model reproduces evolve_layout.check() exactly (same random stream), e.g. 4 whips at 0.354 wavelength 0.72 / 173.3 deg / 8.9 % gross, 225 mm ring at 2.3 GHz with sources 0-30 deg up 26.3 % gross.

(a) Turning a fragile layout about the vertical axis removes its gross errors at equal total time (64 samples split over K): 4 whips at 0.354-1.0 wavelength 7-20 % -> 0.0 % at K=2; 164 mm grid (1.26 wavelength) 14.7 % -> 0 %; 225 mm ring at 2.3 GHz 27.3 % -> 9.9 / 4.3 / 0.6 % at K = 2/4/8. Steps must fill one symmetry sector (45/K deg for a ring of 8); naive 360/K steps land the ring on itself and fix nothing (27.7 % at K=8). However the 225 mm ring failure is an estimator fault: a joint az-el search on one capture gives 0.0 % gross with no motion. Second effect: full-turn steps cancel body-fixed calibration bias to first order (sum of sin(phi - b_n - theta_k) over evenly spaced theta_k is zero): median 0.15 -> 0.03-0.04 deg.

(b) Unknown orientation error passes almost 1:1 into bearing: 0.1 deg is invisible, 0.5 deg gives 0.17-0.21 deg median, 1 deg gives 0.25-0.39 deg (against 0.13 fixed), so motion makes an already-good layout worse unless angles are known to about 0.1 deg. Zero-mean cable-flex drift of 1-10 deg barely matters (worst 0.54 -> 0.70 deg for 4 whips at 10 deg). Neither brings gross errors back.

(c) Panel on an azimuth axis: fixed panel is usable to 60 deg off boresight (0.8 deg median at 2.44 GHz, gain down 4.5 dB), 67 % gross at 90 deg, blind behind. Three stops give 0 % gross over 360 deg (worst-azimuth gain 1.9 / 11.0 dBi at 2.44 / 5.8 GHz), four stops 4.1 / 13.2 dBi. A 360 deg look takes 8-11 s at 30 deg/s with 0.05-0.5 s dwell, 12 s continuous.

(d) A second (tilt) axis is what fixes elevation: flat plate at 1.575 GHz has 1.4-2.2 deg elevation error below 5 deg and cannot tell up from down (about 50 %, free-space whip model); tilted 30 deg at 4 azimuths gives 0.20-0.25 deg and 0 % wrong hemisphere. The panel needs an elevation axis only above about 60 deg.

(e) Polarisation: loss is 20 log10 cos (3 dB at 45, 11.7 dB at 75 deg); DF holds to 85 deg, fails at 90 deg (98 % gross). Rolling about boresight recovers the polarisation angle to 0.3 deg with 3 or more roll angles (2 leaves 22 deg), but it measures power, so 1 dB source fading between captures costs 3 deg and 3 dB costs 8-10 deg.

(f) Whole sphere, random polarisation, 24 captures: fixed plate 41-49 % gross, fixed panel 56 %; azimuth-only plate still 45-47 %, panel 1-2 % but polarisation lost (43-45 deg). Any two-axis path reaches 0 % gross by 360 deg of travel (12 s at 30 deg/s) for the plate, 720 deg for the panel. A third (roll) axis adds little direction accuracy but the best polarisation (panel 5.8 GHz, 720 deg: 1.2 deg against 2.5-4.4 deg; 0.6 deg at 1440 deg). The evolved path beats the plain tumble only for the panel (95th percentile 0.6 against 1.4 deg) and random search is nearly as good: path shape matters little once the sphere is covered. With 1 deg jitter + 0.5 deg axis offset + 3 deg flex all moving paths degrade to 0.6-0.9 deg median (1.1-1.4 deg at 2.44 GHz), still 0 % gross. Too short a tumble is harmful for the panel (180 deg: 13-14 % gross).

findings.claim: rotation_study.az_mc at K=1 reproduces evolve_layout.check() exactly with the same seed (1500 trials): 4 whips r 0.25 wl 0.91/2.7 deg/0.0 %, r 0.354 wl 0.72/173.3/8.9 %, 8 whips r 0.5 wl 0.33/1.0/0.0 %, 225 mm ring of 8 at 2.3 GHz with sources 0-30 deg up 0.15/128.2/26.3 % (evolve_study.md: 0.93/2.62/0.0, 0.75/170.7/10.6, 0.33/0.93/0.0, up to 30 %). The sphere model's single snapshot at SNR+18 dB matches a 64-sample covariance (panel 5.8 GHz 0.30/0.60 against 0.28/0.62 deg).

At equal total time (64 samples split over K orientations inside one symmetry sector) gross errors fall: 4 whips at 0.354/0.45/0.60/1.0 wl 7.2/4.5/9.1/20.4 % -> 0.0 % at K=2; 4x4 grid at 1.26 wl pitch 14.7 % -> 0.0 % at K=2; ring of 8 at 3.3 wl spacing (5.8 GHz) 21.8 -> 1.3 -> 0.0 % at K=1/2/4; 225 mm ring at 2.3 GHz, sources 0-30 deg up, 27.3 -> 9.9 -> 4.3 -> 0.6 % at K=1/2/4/8. Giving every orientation the full 64 samples changes little (0.1 % at K=8).

Steps of 360/K deg map a symmetric layout onto itself and remove no ambiguity: the 225 mm ring stays at 27.7 % gross at K=8, 4-whip rings stay at 5-18 % until K=8 (45 deg steps). Steps must subdivide one symmetry sector (45/K deg for a ring of 8, 90/K for 4 whips or a square grid).

findings.topic: (a) Rotation is not needed for the 225 mm ring failure
findings.claim: The elevated-source failure of the single 225 mm ring is caused by the azimuth-only estimator: the same single capture searched jointly over azimuth and elevation (0-60 deg) gives 0.0 % gross at 2.3 GHz (0.10/0.3 deg) and at 1.8 GHz, with no motion.

Body-fixed per-element phase errors give a first-order bearing bias proportional to sum_n eps_n sin(phi - b_n - theta); summed over orientations evenly spaced over 360 deg this is zero. Simulated: median error 0.15 -> 0.04 deg (K=2, 180 deg) -> 0.03 deg (K=4) for the 225 mm ring; two-ring plate azimuth median 0.13 -> 0.02 deg with 4 azimuths. Applies only to errors that turn with the array, not to site multipath.

Unknown per-move angle error degrades accuracy roughly in proportion and does not restore gross errors: for the two-ring plate at 1.575 GHz (fixed: 0.13/0.4 deg) 0.1 deg error leaves 0.13, 0.5 deg gives 0.17-0.21, 1 deg gives 0.26-0.38 deg median (95th 0.8-1.1). Sparse grid: 0.05 -> 0.16 (0.5 deg) -> 0.29 deg (1 deg) at K=4. For a layout with nothing to fix, moving it with worse than about 0.1 deg angle knowledge makes DF worse than not moving.

Per-element phase drift varying with orientation (modelled as flex x (sin(theta+psi_n) - sin(psi_n)), zero at home; the model is an estimate) of 1 or 3 deg has no measurable effect; 10 deg raises the 4-whip median from 0.49 to 0.60-0.70 deg and leaves the 8- and 16-element layouts within 0.01-0.02 deg. Gross-error rates are unchanged.

findings.topic: (c) Panel on one axis: coverage and gain
findings.claim: Fixed panel azimuth error (median, 2.44/3.5/5.8 GHz): 0.38/0.26/0.16 deg on boresight, 0.79/0.54/0.29 at 60 deg, 1.58/1.05/0.63 at 75 deg, 57-67 % gross at 90 deg, 100 % behind. Stepped to K azimuths: K=2 leaves gaps (67 %/88 % of azimuths within 1 deg), K=3 gives 0 % gross with worst-azimuth gain 1.9/11.0 dBi, K=4 4.1/13.2 dBi, K=8 5.9/15.0 dBi (2.44/5.8 GHz). Element pattern cos^1.5 in power and a -20 dB incoherent back response are estimates.

Time = K x dwell + (K-1)(360/K)/rate (acceleration ignored): at 30 deg/s, 3 stops 8.2/9.5/23 s and 4 stops 9.2/11/29 s for 0.05/0.5/5 s dwell; continuous turn 12 s. At 6 deg/s 40-65 s; at 90 deg/s 2.8-5 s for short dwells. A 64-sample capture at 20 MSPS lasts 3.2 us, in which a 30 deg/s mount turns 1e-4 deg, so capture on the fly does not smear; a 4-slot switched snapshot of 4 ms would turn 0.12 deg.

A 16-element snapshot needs 4 switched slots on 4 channels; capture on the fly is free of smear only if the 4 slots complete within about 1 ms at 30 deg/s (0.03 deg). The real slot time including per-retune recalibration was not modelled.

investigate:mechanics.summary:
Mechanics lens: what it takes to move rev B on one to three axes, and what that costs. Derived numbers come from mech_study.py (this pass) and mech/rotation_mech.py (an earlier pass), both in the scratchpad. External facts carry their source URLs in the findings.

**Payload.** The panel module (tile, core, two bladeRFs, enclosure) is about 1.3 kg (estimate). The whip plate is the heavy part. 500 mm of 2-3 mm aluminium alone weighs 1.06-2.03 kg, so plate + 16 whips + core + radios comes to 2.3-3.3 kg. Mounting the board and radios under the plate balances the whips.

**Loads.** At the DF study's 30 deg/s (60 deg/s²), the acceleration torque is 0.07 N m for the plate and at most 0.02 N m for the panel.
- **Gyroscopic coupling** (Euler's equations) with all three axes at 30 deg/s is 0.016 N m, which is negligible. It reaches 2.3 N m only at camera-gimbal speed (360 deg/s). A fast-spinning "gyroscope" adds load and gives DF nothing.
- **Wind sizes the drives.** Face-on, the plate takes 19 N and up to about 2.4 N m at 11 m/s, and 3.9 N m at 14 m/s. The panel stays at or below 0.3 N m.
- **DIY drive.** A NEMA 17 through SatNOGS-style 54:1 worm-and-belt gearing gives about 10-16 N m and self-locks, but 30 deg/s needs 270 rpm at the motor.
- **Ham rotators.** The Yaesu G-5500DC gives 59/118 N m at 6/2.8 deg/s, with a 3-minute duty limit.
- **Tipping.** A 9 kg tripod set-up with the plate face-on at 1.5 m tips over at about 9 m/s. Staying up at 14 m/s needs about 23 kg in total.

**Joints.** Rev B's conducted PN calibration covers everything after each element. Board-to-radio coax and the tile jumpers can therefore flex in a cable wrap: phase-stable assemblies move ±2-4 deg up to 8 GHz, and the 100 ms calibration slot removes it. Whips, plate and board must still be one rigid rotor.

No DF use needs unlimited rotation:
- I folded the DF study's three-axis tumble into ±180 deg and ran it through that study's own model. DF is unchanged: plate at 1.575 GHz 0.14/0.3 deg against 0.11/0.3; panel at 5.8 GHz 0.25/0.8 against 0.25/1.4 (median/95th).
- The cost is about 1 s of reversals. Stop-and-go pose sets take 1-36 % longer.

So the recommended layout is:
- radios on the rotor;
- only USB and 24 V crossing a cable wrap with less than 360 deg of travel, so a single-turn absolute encoder is never ambiguous.

Slip rings for power are cheap ($20 for 12 circuits at 2 A), but USB 3 slip rings are quote-only. RF rotary joints run from $46 (one channel, 6 GHz) to $1,067 (two channels, 4.5 GHz). A Wi-Fi radio on the rotor sits in the panel's band.

**Orientation knowledge.**
- **Requirement.** The DF study tolerates 0.2 deg of jitter. 1 deg of jitter or a 0.5 deg zero offset multiplies the median error by 2-4.
- **IMUs.** MEMS IMU fusion gives 2-3.5 deg (BNO08x), and motor magnets corrupt magnetometer heading. An accelerometer can still measure mast tilt to about 0.1 deg.
- **Encoders.** AS5048 encoders have 0.06 deg rms noise and ±0.8-1.2 deg of repeatable nonlinearity. Calibrated on the output shaft, they reach about 0.1 deg.
- **Absolute offsets.** ADS-B aircraft at 1090 MHz broadcast GPS positions every second, which gives the plate an absolute reference.
- **Timing.** Latch encoder angles on the RP2040 trigger. At 30 deg/s, 0.1 deg needs time tags within 3.3 ms. Motion during a 64-sample snapshot is about 1e-4 deg. Multi-slot HackRF codes lasting tens of ms need a stop.
- **Stiffness.** A mast must stay above about 8-10 Hz. Otherwise it settles for seconds and tilts by up to degrees in wind.

**"Gyroscopic" rotation in any direction.**
- With a three-ring gimbal or an azimuth-tilt-spin mount, 35-43 % of random constant-rate turns need a joint faster than 3x the body rate, and 10-11 % faster than 10x (gimbal lock).
- Pointing a spin axis first (azimuth + tilt) and then spinning gives constant rotation about any direction, with one joint moving at 1x.
- A sphere on omni-wheels has no singularity, but no cable can reach it, and IMU-only attitude misses the 0.2 deg budget about 10x.

**Cost and effort against REDESIGN** ($50 manual turntable, 520 h):
- **Azimuth turntable** with output encoder and cable wrap: +$50-130, +40-70 h. It also automates the manifold measurement: ±60 x ±60 deg at 5 deg steps takes about 30 min.
- **Tilt axis:** +$100-170 and +30-50 h DIY, or a G-5500DC for about $750.
- **Third axis:** +$100-150, +40-70 h.
- **DJI RS 4 Pro** ($869, 4.5 kg): panel only.
- **Hexapods** (±7.5-21 deg) and **ring gimbals**: not recommended.

Board and radios mounted under the plate put the CG within a few mm of the plate plane (tilt axis self-balanced).

Not a continuous-duty or sub-degree instrument without added output encoders.

SPID RAS lists at EUR 1,240 incl. VAT with 1 deg precision and reed-switch sensing; the RAS/HR (hall sensor, MD-02/HR controller, about EUR 1,435 per SatNOGS) is specified at 0.2 deg, measured steps land within 0.05 deg, but azimuth backlash measured about 0.35 deg.

Sky-Watcher AZ-GTi alt-az mount: 11 lb (5 kg) payload, fastest slew 800x sidereal (about 3.3 deg/s), dual encoders, $525, Wi-Fi control. KrakenRF Discovery Drive az-el: $799, ESP32-S3 with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Hamlib over USB-serial or TCP, limits az 0-360 / el 0-90, shipping estimated August 2026. Both carry a 2.4 GHz radio inside the panel's band, so use their wired interfaces and turn the radio off.

DJI RS 4 Pro: 4.5 kg tested payload (balanced camera), pan 360 deg continuous, tilt -112 to +214 deg, roll -95 to +240 deg, 360 deg/s, gimbal 1.24 kg, 30 Wh battery, $869; the RS SDK (RS 5, RS 4, RS 4 Pro, RS 3 Pro) can set position and read motor and attitude data. Angles come from the gimbal's IMU, so the absolute reference must come from RF.

Commercial hexapods give small angles: PI H-811 +/-10 / +/-10 / +/-21 deg with 5 kg; PI H-824 +/-7.5 / +/-7.5 / +/-12.5 deg with 10 kg; quote-only. A DIY servo Stewart platform was built for about $250, 'two orders of magnitude' below commercial. The DF lens needs 30-90 deg tilts, so hexapods only suit small-angle dithering.

The standard spherical-measurement positioner (a roll axis on an azimuth turntable) covers 360 x 360 deg; NSI-MI systems take 4.5-454 kg depending on CG offset, sold as quoted systems. For array16 the DIY equivalent is az + tilt (+ roll about boresight for polarisation).

At 30 deg/s a 100 ms slot sees 3 deg of wrap travel, about 0.02 deg of phase (ESTIMATE). USB: a through-bore USB slip ring at about $65 (indicative, data rate not stated). 5 Gbps USB 3 slip rings (ByTune, Ingiant) are quote-only. Gigabit Ethernet: about $360 indicative through-bore (DirectIndustry) to $2,821-3,093 (DSTI). Continuous rotation of the bladeRF four-radio mode is therefore not a hobby-priced option.

Single-channel: Pasternack PE1401, DC-6 GHz, VSWR 1.15, 100 rpm average, listed $46.43; Fairview FMRJ1002, DC-18 GHz, about $464. Two-channel DC-4.5 GHz (Zomwave): $1,066.67, 100 rpm. Four-channel DC-6 GHz (Qualwave): quote. Only one channel can sit on an axis without a multi-channel joint, so RF across a continuous joint suits HackRF mode (one combined coax), not four channels.

findings.topic: What crosses the joints (radios on the rotor)
findings.claim: Put the core, tile and radios on the rotor. Then only two USB 3 links (one per bladeRF), the controller's USB and DC power cross; the 10 MHz reference, J51 trigger and all RF stay on the rotor. USB 3 high-power devices draw at most 900 mA (4.5 W) and passive copper USB 3 cables reach about 3 m, which the wrap's service loop eats into. HackRF One streams 8-bit I/Q up to 20 Msps over USB 2.0, so HackRF mode can cross a USB 2 slip ring at full rate. libbladeRF's SC8_Q7 8-bit format targets USB 2-limited hosts, at reduced rates.

Rotor loads: 7.3-13.3 W for the board, about 22 W with two bladeRFs at the USB 3 bus limit, about 40 W with a rotor computer and inner-axis steppers (ESTIMATE). At 5 V that is 4.5-8.1 A (3-5 pairs of 2 A circuits); at 24 V with a 90 % rotor converter it is 1.0-1.9 A (one pair). Send 24 V and make 5 V on the rotor. The rotor's 5 V source must advertise 3 A on USB-C for the board's current interlock.
findings.source: derivation: mech_study.py section 8; board power from REDESIGN.md section 10

findings.topic: Wi-Fi on the rotor is in-band
findings.claim: A +20 dBm Wi-Fi radio 0.15-1 m from the panel puts -2 to -36 dBm on an element at 2.44/5.8 GHz (Friis, element gain 0 or -10 dBi ESTIMATE), against the QAMP's -20 dBm compression point. A battery + Wi-Fi rotor, or a rotator's own ESP32/AZ-GTi Wi-Fi, desensitises the panel. Use wired links, or switch the radios off during captures.
findings.source: derivation: mech/rotation_mech_tables.txt table 8; REDESIGN.md section 5 (QAMP compression)

findings.claim: REDESIGN plans an azimuth-only, +/-60 deg, 5 deg manifold by hand ('a weekend'). On a motorised az-el positioner, a 2-D +/-60 x +/-60 deg grid at 5 deg (625 poses, 38 frequencies 2.3-6 GHz, 50 ms per point, 1 s settle) takes about 30 min; four roll angles take about 2 h; the whip plate (72 azimuths x 7 tilts x 20 frequencies) takes about 18 min. Use the operational mount: the mount's own metal is part of the manifold. A phase centre 100 mm off the axis with the horn at 5 m causes up to 1.15 deg direction error and 0.35 dB swing.
findings.source: derivation: mech_study.py section 9; mech/rotation_mech_tables.txt table 14; REDESIGN.md section 6

findings.topic: Plate sag and whip droop when tilted
findings.claim: With the plate on edge, the rim of a centre-supported 2/3/4 mm aluminium plate sags at most 0.28/0.12/0.06 mm (0.8/0.3/0.2 deg at 2.3 GHz). Stiff 1-2 mm steel whips of 0.18 m droop 0.2-0.8 mm horizontal (at most 0.7 deg at 2.3 GHz, assuming the phase centre moves a third of the tip; ESTIMATE). A 0.5 m whip droops 48 mm and rubber-duck whips on springs must be measured. Tilting the plate therefore needs stiff whips, and the manifold should be measured at several tilts.
findings.source: derivation: mech_study.py section 10 (cantilever bounds; E = 69 GPa from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6061_aluminium_alloy; steel ESTIMATE)

findings.claim: Stepper choppers and switch-mode converters near a receiver with 1-2 dB noise figure can add spurs; SatNOGS already fits ferrites on its motor leads. Mitigations: keep drivers under the ground plate or off the rotor, use twisted, ferrited motor leads, run TMC2209 StealthChop2 (256-microstep interpolation, StallGuard4 sensorless stall detection), and cut motor current during captures where a self-locking worm holds the load. The level is unquantified: measure it with the board's own receiver.
findings.source: https://wiki.satnogs.org/SatNOGS_Rotator_v3 ; https://www.analog.com/en/tmc2209 ; level is an ESTIMATE to be measured

findings.claim: Hazards by priority: (1) tip-over in wind with the plate: ballast 23-45 kg or guy lines, or take the plate down; (2) crush and pinch at worm-driven axes (10-137 N m): guards, current limits, stall detection, an e-stop; (3) whip tips at eye height when the plate tilts: tip caps and a keep-out zone; (4) cable-wrap overtravel: hard stops plus absolute encoders with under 360 deg of travel; (5) duty cycle: the G-5500DC allows 3 minutes continuous; (6) electrical: 24 V SELV, fused, no mains on the rotor, care with a rotor LiPo, mast down in storms. Kinetic energy is trivial at 30 deg/s: plate rim 0.13 m/s, 0.01 J.

findings.topic: What each axis buys (DF lens, for the cost side)
findings.claim: One azimuth axis: the panel reaches 360 deg with 3-4 stops (0 % gross; 95th 0.9 deg at 2.44 GHz, 0.5 deg at 5.8 GHz) and the elevated-source failure of the 225 mm ring disappears. That failure is also fixed in software alone by an az-el search (0 % gross with no motion). Two axes (tilting the plate 30-60 deg, or az + tilt paths) give elevation, up/down discrimination and whole-sphere DF (median 0.13-0.16 deg at L = 720 deg). A third axis adds little: plate median 0.11 against 0.13 deg; it mainly sharpens the panel's polarisation and 95th percentile.

findings.topic: Cost and effort deltas against REDESIGN
findings.claim: Basis: REDESIGN's $50 manual turntable and 520 h; part prices from the findings above; other parts and all hours are ESTIMATES. (A) Azimuth turntable: NEMA 17 + TMC2209 + worm or belt, AS5048A on the output, <360 deg cable wrap, RP2040-latched; +$50-130, +40-70 h; doubles as the automated manifold turntable. (B) Add a tilt axis with counterweight and encoder: +$150-300 total, +70-120 h; SatNOGS v3 + encoders +$285-395; G-5500DC + encoders and interface about +$800, +25-50 h, but 6 / 2.8 deg/s and 3-min duty. (C) Add roll or spin: +$100-150, +40-70 h. (D) DJI RS 4 Pro for the panel only: +$869, +25-50 h. (E) Hexapod: DIY about $250, +60-120 h, angles too small; commercial quote-only. (F) Three-ring continuous gimbal: +$500-1,000, +200-400 h, slip rings on every axis and gimbal lock. (G) Atlas sphere: +$400-900, +200-400 h, attitude unsolved. Recommendation: A at build step 4, B if elevation or polarisation matters, skip F and G.

open_questions: Real masses and whip type: weigh the plate, whips, board and radios in their cases. Rubber-duck or telescopic whips may droop several mm when tilted, which decides whether the plate can take a tilt axis at all.

The built mount's first mode and damping are unknown. Tap-test it with an accelerometer or gyro: below about 8 Hz, stop-and-go needs seconds of settling per pose or jerk-limited or input-shaped moves.
Does the owner want on-the-fly capture (fine for 64-sample snapshots) or long integrations? HackRF-mode codes over tens of ms and weak-signal integrations need stops or 5 deg/s or less.
Where and in what wind will it run (rooftop or tripod, mast height)? That sets ballast (23-45 kg for the plate), mast tube size and whether the plate is removed above Beaufort 5.

DJI RS 4 Pro holding torque and the accuracy of attitude read through the RS SDK are unpublished; test with the panel before relying on it. Can the AZ-GTi and Discovery Drive Wi-Fi be switched off when driven over serial?
How much stepper-driver and converter noise reaches the 0.4-6 GHz chain is not quantified; measure it with the board's own receiver with motors energised, idle and off.
Will the two bladeRFs stream reliably at 4 x 20 MSPS through a cable-wrapped USB 3 run longer than about 3 m (active or optical extenders)? If not, the Mac moves onto the mount, or the rate drops.
The radar horn stays fixed beside the array: its TX coax would flex through the wrap and the TX-RX isolation geometry changes with pose. Is radar ever wanted while the array moves?
The cost and effort deltas are estimates. Build hours for SatNOGS v3 and a DIY tilt stage should be checked against community build logs before committing.
